reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / KDIGO
clinicalPearls: A rare and poorly understood syndrome of severe, often disabling loin (flank) pain accompanied by haematuria, in the absence of an identifiable urological or glomerular cause
It is fundamentally a diagnosis of exclusion after stones, tumours, infection, obstruction, and glomerular disease have been ruled out
The pain may be unilateral or bilateral, can be constant or episodic, and is frequently out of proportion to any objective findings
The haematuria is usually microscopic but may be macroscopic, and dysmorphic red cells can occur, sometimes suggesting a subtle glomerular contribution
It predominantly affects younger women and is often associated with substantial psychological distress and impaired quality of life
Proposed mechanisms include abnormalities of the glomerular basement membrane allowing red cell leakage, microcrystalluria, and intrarenal vascular or nociceptive factors, but none is definitive
Management is challenging and centres on multidisciplinary pain control and support, with cautious use of invasive interventions given inconsistent results
Kidney function and long-term renal survival are generally preserved, which is important for reassurance
reference.pathophysiology: The cause of loin pain haematuria syndrome remains uncertain and is likely multifactorial. Leading hypotheses propose that structural abnormalities of the glomerular basement membrane permit red blood cells to pass into the tubules, where they may obstruct flow and distend the renal capsule, generating pain. Other proposed contributors include microcrystal deposition, intrarenal vasospasm or microvascular disease, and heightened visceral nociceptive signalling. Because objective pathology is minimal, central sensitisation and chronic pain mechanisms are thought to play an important role in perpetuating symptoms. The absence of progressive structural damage explains why kidney function is usually maintained.
additionalDifferentials: IgA nephropathy and thin basement membrane nephropathy
Ureteric obstruction or ureteropelvic junction abnormality
additionalInvestigations: Urinalysis and microscopy for red cell morphology and casts
Cross-sectional imaging (CT) to exclude stones, obstruction, and masses
Cystoscopy and urine cytology where malignancy or bladder source is a concern
Assessment of proteinuria and kidney function, with biopsy considered in selected cases
Vascular imaging to exclude nutcracker phenomenon when suspected
redFlags: New or changing haematuria that could indicate malignancy
Fever or systemic signs suggesting infection
Findings of obstruction or a renal mass on imaging
reference.prognosis: Kidney function is typically preserved and the syndrome is not life-threatening, but the pain is often chronic, relapsing, and difficult to control, with a considerable impact on quality of life and mental health.
pitfalls: Making the diagnosis before adequately excluding treatable structural and glomerular causes
Escalating opioids and invasive procedures with limited evidence of benefit
Dismissing patients' pain as purely psychological
Missing an alternative such as nutcracker syndrome or a subtle glomerulonephritis
management: Explain that no disease-specific drug cures the syndrome and that care is symptomatic once stones, tumour, infection, obstruction and glomerular disease have been excluded
Anchor treatment in a multidisciplinary chronic-pain programme using simple analgesia and neuropathic agents such as tricyclic antidepressants or gabapentinoids, minimising escalating opioid use
Provide psychological therapy such as cognitive behavioural therapy to address the central sensitisation and associated distress
Offer interventional analgesia such as splanchnic or coeliac plexus nerve blocks or catheter-based techniques in refractory pain, with realistic expectations of benefit

Reserve ablative and surgical options such as renal denervation, autotransplantation or nephrectomy for carefully selected refractory cases, counselling that results are unpredictable and pain may recur
Monitor renal function and blood pressure periodically, reassuring that kidney function is typically preserved, and avoid repeated invasive investigation
Refer jointly to nephrology and a specialist pain service, escalating when pain becomes disabling or opioid dependence develops
